title: The Mystery of the Bouncing Bells
markdown:
Tucked in the very highest mountains, where the clouds gathered for tea and the wind sang lullabies to the fir trees, lay a valley called Lumina. Gardens clung to the sides like colourful ribbons. Lakes shimmered with captured-starlight habits. Narrow passes wound like a playful coil. The valley bells, usually, chimed a gentle ding-dong, a soft heart-sound, nothing that scattered sugar.

Wizard Caspar lived there, not the booming thunder-wielding sort but quiet and clever. His beard was the colour of a stormy sky, and little grey fluff-balls clung to it like tiny misplaced sheep. Spectacles made a career of sliding down his nose while he peered at ancient scrolls. His dearest companion was Clover, a sleek black cat with eyes like polished emeralds and a purr that could mend a broken quill. Her tail was a barometer: slow swish for contentment, sharp flick for mild concern.

One crisp morning the air was rudely interrupted. The bells began to ring — not ring so much as jangle and clang and ding-dong-dilly-dally in a most unseemly fashion. Sunrise: metallic clatter, sleepy valley jarred. Noon: a dreadful racket that shut the birds up. Afternoon tea: sugar lumps scattering, cups rattling in their saucers. Oh, the din.

“Disaster!” declared the mayor, face as red as a ripe mountain berry. The baker wrung flour-dusted hands. The shepherd clutched his head; the sheep looked equally bewildered. Everyone was in a tizzy. They whispered a curse on the wind, a dragon’s particularly loud sneeze, a magical hiccup from the Great Mountain Spirit. Grand gestures and stern letters were prepared. The air, usually birdsong, thickened with frustration.

Caspar stroked Clover and watched. No rush. “Emotionally annoying,” he told the cat. Clover’s motorboat purr agreed. “A puzzle. Not a panic.”

He knew the goblin for odd mechanics. Glimble’s workshop smelled of burnt sugar and ozone, cogs and starlight wire, things that worked sometimes too well.

“A word.” Clover padded. “Mind the anti-gravity teapot,” Glimble said, goggles smudged, popping from the hum. “It drifts.”

Caspar navigated organised chaos. “The bells will not stop. The valley has decided on doom.”

Glimble’s eyes went wide and pleased. “Working? Perfectly?”

“What is working?”

“The Grand Bell Ringer 3000. Installed last week. Pressure plates in the paths. Alert the valley to important events.” A beam. “I was hoping for a particularly large avalanche.”

Clover: a questioning mrow.

“And the significant sustained pressure of late?” Caspar asked, amusement arriving without being invited.

Glimble pointed at the high pastures. A new herd of exceptionally fluffy, exceptionally bouncy mountain goats had been introduced. Their hopping was, as it happened, exactly the pressure the plates had dreamed of. Every caper rang the valley.

“Happy goats,” Caspar said.

“Enthusiastic!” Glimble chirped. A spring left his hair.

Caspar sighed the fond kind. “Ingenious. Inconvenient. Tea has suffered.” Mist moved through firs. “We calm the impact. We do not uninvent the goats, or you.”

“Extra-soft moss? The spongy cushioning sort?”

Glimble produced loads from a green pile.

They climbed quietly, Clover supervising with a critic’s eye, and packed the plates in springy thickness. Goat hooves met moss and made only a polite thud. Bounces stayed bounces. Bells, deprived of their cue, remembered silence.

Birdsong clocked back in. Goats bleated, unaware of their career in percussion. Some folk swore they could hear flowers growing, which was their business. Relief filled ears that had been full of clang.

Dusk put rose and lavender on Caspar’s study. Clover took his lap. He did not explain cleverness to the room. He poured the tea that had been waiting since noon, and Clover’s purr kept a better time than Glimble’s plates. Tomorrow, perhaps, they would aim the invention at actual avalanches. Tonight the moss stayed on the mountain, doing the one job worth doing.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
